usage: to be startled / get a shock
The single most common pairing. 깜짝 almost always attaches to 놀라다 — treat them as one chunk.
A reflex exclamation when something startles you. Often stretched to 아이 깜짝이야 or 깜짝 놀랐잖아.
깜짝 + noun = 'surprise ~'. Also 깜짝 파티 (surprise party), 깜짝 방문 (surprise visit), 깜짝 발표 (surprise announcement).
Doubled 깜짝깜짝 means repeatedly flinching, e.g. from loud noises or being on edge.
examples: 깜짝 놀랐어요.
You startled me / I got a shock.
The bare-minimum sentence; memorize 깜짝 놀라다 as one unit before anything else.
갑자기 뒤에서 불러서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
You called me from behind so suddenly that I got startled.
Note 불러서 (because you called) gives the cause; 깜짝 sits right before the verb it intensifies.
뒤에서 친구가 '왁!' 하는 바람에 깜짝이야, 하고 소리를 질렀어요.
My friend went 'Boo!' behind me, and I yelped 'You scared me!'
Real-situation: 깜짝이야 used as the live spoken reaction inside a story (반말 narration).
nuance: 깜짝 captures the split-second jolt of being startled, not a gradual surprise — it is the body's flinch the instant something pops up. Compare it with 갑자기 'suddenly': 갑자기 only marks that an event happened without warning (timing), while 깜짝 names the startle reaction itself, so they often appear together (갑자기 ~해서 깜짝 놀랐다). The dividing line vs 놀라다 alone is intensity-of-onset: 깜짝 forces the 'jump' reading. Its strongest collocation is 깜짝 놀라다, and the standalone 깜짝이야! is something you will say constantly. As a noun-modifier it means 'surprise ~' (깜짝 세일, 깜짝 방문). The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 깜짝 as a verb: there is no 깜짝하다 — 깜짝 is an adverb and always needs 놀라다 (or another verb) behind it.

mistakes: Saying 깜짝했어요 as if 깜짝 were a verb. 깜짝하다 is not a real word; you must say 깜짝 놀랐어요 — the adverb 깜짝 plus the verb 놀라다.
Using 깜짝 to mean 'suddenly' in a neutral sentence like '갑자기 비가 왔어요'. 깜짝 carries the startle/jump nuance, so for plain unexpected timing you need 갑자기, not 깜짝.
Reaching for 놀라운 (amazing/remarkable) when you mean the jolt. 놀랍다 describes something impressive; 깜짝 놀라다 is the physical flinch — don't swap them.

usage: The textbook frame. The subject is 가슴 (chest/heart), and 두근두근 describes how it beats.
Pairs with 설레다 (to be thrilled) for positive anticipation — crushes, trips, first days.
Pairs with 떨리다 (to tremble/be nervous) for the anxious side — auditions, results, exams.
The single-action verb 두근거리다 is the more literary, write-it-down equivalent of 두근두근하다.
examples: 가슴이 두근두근해요.
My heart is pounding.
The core sentence — note 가슴이 (heart, as subject) + 두근두근하다 as a descriptive verb.
좋아하는 사람을 만나면 가슴이 두근두근해요.
When I meet the person I like, my heart pounds.
Everyday romantic context; 만나면 (when/if I meet) sets up the trigger for the flutter.
첫 출근날이라 아침부터 두근두근하면서도 긴장됐어요.
It was my first day at work, so from the morning I was both fluttery and nervous.
Real-situation: shows 두근두근 layered with 긴장되다, the mixed excited-anxious feeling a newcomer knows.
nuance: 두근두근 is the sound-feeling of a fast heartbeat (의태어/의성어) and works for BOTH happy anticipation and anxious nerves — context and the partner verb decide which. The key contrast is with 긴장되다 'to be tense/nervous': 긴장되다 is flatly negative stress, whereas 두근두근 is warmer and bodily, often carrying 설렘 (sweet excitement), so a crush or a trip is 두근두근 but rarely just 긴장돼요. It is also distinct from 떨리다 (to physically tremble): 떨려요 can be visible shaking, while 두근두근 is specifically the heart's thumping. Use it adverbially (두근두근 떨려요) or as 두근두근하다. The pitfall for English speakers is mapping it to a pounding heart from physical exertion — after running, Koreans say 숨차다 or 헐떡거리다, not 두근두근, which is reserved for emotional racing. Also remember the subject is usually 가슴/심장, not 'I'.

mistakes: Using it for a heart pounding from running or stairs. Exertion is 숨차다 / 헐떡거리다; 두근두근 is the emotional racing of excitement or nerves only.
Assuming it is only fear. 두근두근 strongly implies 설렘 (excitement), so 'I'm scared' alone is 무서워요 — 두근두근 adds the thrilled-anticipation color.
Saying 나는 두근두근해요 with yourself as subject when you really want the heart as subject. The natural frame is 가슴이/심장이 두근두근해요; the heart does the pounding.

usage: The core collocation, for stars, polished surfaces, jewelry, and eager eyes.
Descriptive verb form: 청소했더니 바닥이 반짝반짝해요 (after cleaning, the floor is sparkling).
Describes bright, eager eyes — a child's, or someone lit up with excitement.
Single 반짝 = a brief one-off flash, hence 반짝 세일 (a short, sudden sale) and 반짝 인기 (a brief fad).
examples: 별이 반짝반짝 빛나요.
The stars are twinkling.
The simplest frame — 반짝반짝 directly modifies 빛나다.
설거지를 끝내니까 그릇이 반짝반짝해요.
After I finished the dishes, the bowls are sparkling clean.
Everyday context; here 반짝반짝하다 works as a stand-alone descriptive verb, no 빛나다 needed.
면접관 앞에서 아이가 눈을 반짝반짝하면서 자기 꿈을 이야기했어요.
In front of the interviewer, the child talked about her dream with sparkling, eager eyes.
Real-situation: 눈이 반짝반짝 for the 'lit-up, eager' look rather than literal shine.
nuance: 반짝반짝 evokes light bouncing off something repeatedly — stars, a just-mopped floor, jewelry, or wide eager eyes. It is famously the opening of the Korean 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star' (반짝반짝 작은 별), so it instantly sounds storybook-warm. Two contrasts matter. First, single 반짝 means a brief, one-time flash (반짝 세일, 반짝 스타), whereas doubled 반짝반짝 means continuous glittering. Second, do not confuse it with 번쩍: 반짝 is small, cute, decorative sparkle, while 번쩍 (its 'big brother' with the heavier 어 vowel) is a sudden powerful flash — lightning 번쩍, or 정신이 번쩍 들다 'to snap wide awake'. Korean's vowel symbolism (bright ㅏ/ㅗ = small & cute, dark ㅓ/ㅜ = big & strong) is doing real work here. The English-speaker pitfall is using 반짝반짝 for steady brightness like a lamp; plain brightness is 밝다, and 반짝반짝 specifically requires the glitter/twinkle of reflected, intermittent light.

Mixing up 반짝 (small cute sparkle) with 번쩍 (a big sudden flash like lightning). The darker vowel in 번쩍 signals something larger and more startling.
Treating 반짝반짝 and single 반짝 as identical. Doubled = ongoing twinkling; single 반짝 = one brief flash, as in 반짝 세일 (flash sale).

usage: The default frame. 비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the full natural phrase for heavy streaming rain.
For tears running down the face in lines — pairs with 흐르다 (to flow).
For sweat streaming in the heat — 등에 땀이 주룩주룩 (sweat pouring down one's back).
Pairs with 쏟아지다 (to gush) to stress sheer volume of rain.
examples: 비가 주룩주룩 내려요.
It's pouring (rain).
The base weather sentence; 내리다 is the most natural verb for falling rain.
아침부터 비가 주룩주룩 내려서 우산을 챙겼어요.
It's been pouring since morning, so I grabbed an umbrella.
Everyday cause-effect: -아서 (because) links the rain to grabbing the umbrella.
퇴근길에 갑자기 비가 주룩주룩 쏟아져서 옷이 다 젖었어요.
On the way home from work, rain suddenly poured down and my clothes got soaked.
Real-situation: 주룩주룩 쏟아지다 emphasizing a heavy downpour that drenches you.
nuance: 주룩주룩 describes liquid running down in steady, continuous streams — most often heavy rain, but equally tears and sweat. It is genuinely heavy and unbroken, which is what separates it from the soft drizzle words 부슬부슬 / 보슬보슬 (a fine misty rain you barely need an umbrella for). It also differs from 후두둑, the brief pattering of the first fat drops, and from 주르륵, a single quick run-down (one tear, water down a window); 주룩주룩 is the sustained, repeated version. The natural verb is 내리다 for rain and 흐르다 for tears/sweat. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 주룩주룩 with 오다 by analogy to 'rain comes' — 비가 주룩주룩 와요 is acceptable, but 내리다 sounds cleaner, and crucially you should NOT use 주룩주룩 for light rain at all. During Korea's 장마 (monsoon) season this is the word you'll see in every weather chat.

Defaulting to 비가 주룩주룩 와요. It is not wrong, but 비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the more natural pairing native speakers prefer.
Pairing 주룩주룩 with snow. Snow doesn't 'stream down' — heavy snow is 펑펑 (눈이 펑펑 와요), so reserve 주룩주룩 for rain, tears, and sweat.

usage: Very common: hard, body-shaking sobbing, not a few tears.
Big, fast snowfall in fat flakes. 눈이 펑펑 와요 / 펑펑 내려요.
To splurge / blow money freely, usually with a faintly disapproving tone.
Single 펑 is the actual burst sound — a balloon, a firework, a cork.
examples: 펑펑 울었어요.
I cried my eyes out.
The base sentence; 펑펑 signals serious sobbing, far stronger than 조금 울었어요.
밤새 눈이 펑펑 와서 길이 하얘졌어요.
It snowed heavily all night, so the roads turned white.
Everyday weather; 펑펑 with 눈 specifically means thick, fast snowfall.
월급 받자마자 돈을 펑펑 쓰더니 월말에 카드값 때문에 후회하더라고요.
She blew money the moment she got paid, then regretted it at month-end over the card bill.
Real-situation: 돈을 펑펑 쓰다 with the disapproving 'splurge-then-regret' arc.
nuance: 펑펑 has three everyday senses tied together by the image of something bursting out in abundance: crying hard (펑펑 울다), heavy snowfall (눈이 펑펑 와요), and splurging money (돈을 펑펑 쓰다). Context makes the meaning instantly clear, because each sense has a fixed partner verb (울다 / 오다·내리다 / 쓰다). Two contrasts to lock in. For crying, compare 엉엉 울다 (loud wailing, mouth open) — 펑펑 stresses the gushing flow of tears, 엉엉 the loud sound; both mean hard crying and often interchange. For snow, 펑펑 means big abundant flakes, unlike the rain word 주룩주룩, which never describes snow. The single 펑 is the literal 'pop/bang' of a burst (a vowel-darker, bigger cousin of 팡). The English-speaker pitfall is using 펑펑 for rain — heavy rain is 주룩주룩 or 쏟아지다, and 펑펑 with weather means snow only.

Assuming 펑펑 울다 is mild crying. It means serious, hard sobbing — for just a couple of tears use 살짝 울다 or 눈물이 났어요.
Treating 돈을 펑펑 쓰다 as neutral 'spending'. It carries a wasteful/reckless tone; plain spending is just 돈을 쓰다, so don't use 펑펑 unless you mean to imply splurging.

usage: Core usage: moving quietly on soft feet so as not to be noticed.
Approaching quietly, often to surprise someone or like a cat stalking prey.
Entering quietly, e.g. coming home late and not wanting to wake anyone.
Leaving a room/place without being noticed.
examples: 살금살금 걸었어요.
I walked on tiptoe / I crept along.
The base frame: 살금살금 directly modifies a verb of motion.
아기가 자고 있어서 살금살금 걸어 나왔어요.
The baby was sleeping, so I tiptoed out.
Everyday considerate movement; -아서 gives the reason for being quiet.
고양이가 참새를 향해 살금살금 다가가다가 결국 들켜서 참새가 날아가 버렸어요.
The cat crept toward the sparrow but got spotted in the end, and the sparrow flew off.
Real-situation: stalking with 다가가다, the most natural verb for closing in quietly.
nuance: 살금살금 describes moving deliberately and softly so you won't be heard or seen — tiptoeing past a sleeping roommate, a cat stalking a bird, sneaking home late. It carries a slightly playful, cautious feel and pairs with verbs of motion (걷다, 다가가다, 들어가다, 나오다). The sharp contrast to memorize is 슬금슬금: 슬금슬금 means edging away gradually and sheepishly, usually to dodge blame or slip out of a situation (혼날까 봐 슬금슬금 도망쳤다), so it foregrounds 'sneaking off to avoid something', while 살금살금 foregrounds 'quiet footsteps so as not to make noise'. It also differs from 슬며시/슬쩍, which mean doing something subtly or on the sly (slipping a note, a quiet smile) rather than literal quiet walking. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for fast quiet movement: stealthy-but-quick is 후다닥 or 잽싸게, whereas 살금살금 is inherently slow and careful.

Using it for fast quiet movement. Quick-and-quiet is 후다닥 / 잽싸게; 살금살금 is deliberately slow and tiptoeing.
Pairing it with non-motion verbs. 살금살금 needs a verb of moving (걷다, 다가가다); you can't say 살금살금 말하다 for whispering — that's 소곤소곤 / 속삭이다.

usage: Springing up in a flustered burst, e.g. when you oversleep and bolt out of bed.
to get ready in a rush
Throwing yourself together fast and a little frantically.
Eating very fast, gulping it down before running off.
Running off suddenly, often half in a panic.
examples: 후다닥 일어났어요.
I jumped up in a flash.
The base frame: 후다닥 + a quick action verb.
늦잠을 자서 후다닥 준비하고 나왔어요.
I overslept, so I got ready in a mad rush and left.
Everyday morning scramble; -아서 links oversleeping to the frantic prep.
바퀴벌레가 갑자기 나타나는 바람에 다들 비명을 지르며 후다닥 도망갔어요.
A cockroach suddenly appeared, so everyone screamed and bolted.
Real-situation: 후다닥 도망가다 for a sudden, slightly comic panic-dash.
nuance: 후다닥 conveys doing something in a fast, slightly frantic burst — jumping up, scrambling to get ready, dashing off. The defining flavor is speed PLUS commotion or fluster, which is exactly what separates it from the neutral 빨리 'quickly' and from 잽싸게 'nimbly/deftly': 빨리 is plain speed and 잽싸게 implies smooth, skillful quickness, whereas 후다닥 implies a flustered scramble, often with noise or panic. It is also distinct from 허둥지둥, which stresses being flustered and disorganized (flailing, losing things in your haste); 후다닥 keeps the focus on the quick burst of action itself. Note 후다닥 has the heavy ㅜ/ㅏ vowels of a bigger, more energetic motion, versus the lighter 호다닥. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is pairing it with calm, careful, or slow actions — it clashes with 천천히 and with deliberate tasks, so use it only when there's a hurried, scrambling feel.

Pairing it with slow or careful actions. 후다닥 천천히 or 후다닥 + a meticulous task is contradictory — the word demands a hurried burst.

usage: Core collocation: turning continuously in circles (intransitive).
The everyday way to say you feel dizzy: 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요.
Transitive: spinning an object, e.g. twirling a pen or a hula hoop.
Shorter 빙빙 is a near-synonym with a slightly faster, looser feel.
examples: 팽이가 빙글빙글 돌아요.
The top spins round and round.
The base frame: 빙글빙글 directly modifies 돌다.
갑자기 일어났더니 머리가 빙글빙글 돌았어요.
I stood up suddenly and my head started spinning.
Everyday dizziness; -았더니 (did X, and as a result) links standing up to the dizzy spell.
회전목마를 너무 오래 탔는지 내려서도 세상이 빙글빙글 도는 것 같았어요.
Maybe I rode the carousel too long — even after getting off, the world seemed to spin.
Real-situation: 빙글빙글 돌다 extended to a lingering whirling sensation.
nuance: 빙글빙글 describes smooth, continuous rotation in place — a spinning top, a carousel, or a dizzy head whirling. For dizziness, 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요 is the natural everyday phrase you'd give a doctor or friend, and 어지러워요 (I'm dizzy) is its plain companion. The crucial contrast is with 데굴데굴: 빙글빙글 is rotating on the spot, while 데굴데굴 is a round object ROLLING ALONG the ground (a ball, a dropped tangerine) — same idea of turning, totally different path. Within the spinning family, the shorter 빙빙 is interchangeable in most cases but feels a touch quicker and is common in 빙빙 돌리다 / 빙빙 돌려 말하다 (to beat around the bush), whereas the darker-vowel 뱅뱅 suggests tighter, smaller circles. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is using 빙글빙글 for a single half-turn: one turn is just 돌다, and 빙글빙글 requires repeated, ongoing rotation.

usage: Core pairing with 기침하다 (to cough); the two go together naturally.
Verb form for ongoing coughing fits, written as one word.
Light spoken form, often about a child. 아이가 콜록콜록해요.
Single 콜록 is one cough sound; doubling it = repeated coughing.
examples: 콜록콜록 기침해요.
I'm coughing (cough-cough).
The base frame: 콜록콜록 directly modifies 기침하다.
감기에 걸려서 밤새 콜록콜록 기침했어요.
I caught a cold and coughed all night long.
Everyday clinic/pharmacy line; 감기에 걸리다 (to catch a cold) is the standard collocation.
옆자리 사람이 마스크도 안 쓰고 콜록콜록거려서 자리를 옮겼어요.
The person next to me kept coughing without even a mask, so I moved seats.
Real-situation: 콜록콜록거리다 in a slightly annoyed observation about someone else.
nuance: 콜록콜록 is the onomatopoeia for repeated coughing and pairs naturally with 기침하다, or stands alone as 콜록콜록거리다 / 콜록콜록하다. It is the word you'll actually use to describe cold symptoms to a 약사 (pharmacist) or 의사 (doctor), alongside 기침이 나요 (I have a cough). A single dry cough is 콜록; the doubled form signals ongoing coughing fits. Two distinctions help. First, 콜록콜록 vs 쿨럭쿨럭: both exist, but the darker-vowel 쿨럭 suggests a deeper, heavier chest cough, while 콜록 is the lighter, standard form you should default to. Second, do not confuse coughing with sneezing — a sneeze is 에취 (the sound) or 재채기 (the noun/act), never 콜록콜록. usage: Core collocation: deep, sound sleep. 쿨쿨 almost always attaches to 자다.
Dropping into deep sleep (잠들다 = to fall asleep).
Progressive: someone is sound asleep right now.
to snooze / breathe heavily in sleep
Verb form, sometimes implying soft, audible sleeping breaths.
examples: 쿨쿨 자요.
(He) is sleeping soundly / zzz.
The base frame: 쿨쿨 directly modifies 자다.
주말에는 늦게까지 쿨쿨 자고 싶어요.
On weekends I want to sleep in soundly until late.
Everyday wish; -고 싶다 (want to) attaches to the verb after 쿨쿨.
남편은 옆에서 아기가 우는데도 모르고 쿨쿨 자고 있더라고요.
My husband was fast asleep, oblivious, even though the baby was crying right next to him.
Real-situation: 쿨쿨 자다 with a fond-but-exasperated tone about dead-to-the-world sleep.
nuance: 쿨쿨 is the cozy onomatopoeia for sleeping deeply and soundly — the Korean equivalent of 'zzz'. It pairs almost exclusively with 자다 / 잠들다 and carries a warm, slightly cute tone, so you'd use it for a tired roommate napping or a pet snoozing, not for a clinical sleep report (수면 / 숙면 are the formal words). Two contrasts sharpen it. First, 쿨쿨 means genuinely deep sleep, unlike 꾸벅꾸벅 졸다, which is nodding off / dozing while basically awake (on the subway, in a meeting). Second, do not equate it with snoring: heavy snoring is 드르렁드르렁 or the verb 코를 골다, whereas 쿨쿨 is peaceful, gentle sleeping — at most softly audible breathing, not a sawing snore. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 쿨쿨 to mean any kind of resting; for a quick nap-while-sitting you want 졸다, and for 'go to bed/sleep' in a neutral sense you simply use 자다 — 쿨쿨 specifically adds the 'out cold, sound asleep' picture.

usage: Core collocation: a round thing rolling on the ground (구르다 = to roll).
Rolling off in a direction, away from you.
to roll around on the floor
Often used jokingly for laughing hard or writhing in pain on the floor.
Tense/emphatic variant 떼굴떼굴 for heavier, bigger, more forceful rolling.
examples: 공이 데굴데굴 굴러가요.
The ball is rolling away.
The base frame: 데굴데굴 + 굴러가다 for a thing rolling off.
공이 책상에서 떨어져서 데굴데굴 굴러갔어요.
The ball fell off the desk and rolled away.
Everyday object mishap; -아서 chains 'fell off' to 'rolled away'.
그 개그가 너무 웃겨서 다 같이 바닥에서 데굴데굴 굴렀어요.
That joke was so funny we all rolled on the floor laughing.
Real-situation: the idiomatic 'ROFL' use, 바닥에서 데굴데굴 구르다.
nuance: 데굴데굴 describes a round object rolling along a surface — a ball, a dropped tangerine, a marble — and by extension a person 'rolling on the floor' laughing hard or doubled over in pain (바닥에서 데굴데굴 구르다, the Korean ROFL). The defining feature is travel along the ground, which is exactly the line against 빙글빙글: 빙글빙글 spins IN PLACE (a top, a dizzy head), while 데굴데굴 always moves the object ALONG. Size matters too: for tiny things rolling — a bead, a single tear, a marble down a slope — 또르르 is the natural choice, whereas 데굴데굴 fits ball-sized objects; and the tenser 떼굴떼굴 amps up the weight/force. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja, but notice the bright ㅔ/ㅜ vowels give it a rounder, friendlier feel than its heavier cousin 떼굴떼굴. The English-speaker pitfall is using 데굴데굴 for spinning in place; if nothing travels across the floor, you want 빙글빙글, not 데굴데굴.

usage: Core collocation: scanning the surroundings (둘러보다 = to look around).
The 거리다 form, just as common as the doubled adverb in speech and writing.
Descriptive verb form: looking this way and that.
Pairs with 주위 / 사방 (surroundings, all directions).
examples: 두리번두리번 둘러봤어요.
I looked all around.
The base frame: 두리번두리번 + 둘러보다.
친구를 찾느라 카페에서 두리번두리번했어요.
I looked around the cafe searching for my friend.
Everyday searching; -느라 (busy doing X) gives the reason for scanning.
처음 와 본 동네라 출구가 어디인지 두리번거리다가 결국 지나가는 분께 길을 물었어요.
It was my first time in the area, so I looked around for the exit and finally asked a passerby for directions.
Real-situation: 두리번거리다 for a lost newcomer getting their bearings.
nuance: 두리번두리번 captures turning your head this way and that to take in your surroundings — searching for someone, getting your bearings when lost, or wide-eyed in a new place. It implies a slightly anxious or curious, restless scanning, and the 거리다 form 두리번거리다 is every bit as common as the doubled adverb. Two contrasts pin it down. Against a single glance: one quick look is 흘끗/힐끗 보다 or 쳐다보다, whereas 두리번두리번 is repeated looking in multiple directions. Against 기웃거리다 (기웃기웃): 기웃거리다 is craning to PEEK INTO a specific spot — a shop window, someone's doorway, often a bit nosy — while 두리번두리번 is broad, all-around scanning of open space. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja; note that the verb pair 둘러보다 'to look around' is the neutral action and 두리번두리번 adds the vivid restless-scanning picture. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for a single directed look; reserve 두리번두리번 for head-turning in several directions.
